extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating patentability (novelty/obviousness/indefiniteness) of apparatus claims, computer‑implemented functional limitations, material‑worked‑upon limitations, process claims with novel products, and Markush groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process prior art handling (102/103 alternative rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art discloses a product that reasonably appears identical or only slightly different from a product claimed in a product‑by‑process claim, a rejection alternatively based on 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 is fair and acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should note that reliance on alternative grounds (102 or 103) does not eliminate the need to explain both the anticipation and obviousness aspects of the rejections. The Patent Office is not equipped to manufacture and physically compare products made by myriad processes, so examiners may rely on alternative statutory grounds but must explain both aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency for functional limitations in apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functional limitation in an apparatus claim is an inherent characteristic of the prior art structure, the examiner should explain that the prior art structure inherently possesses the claimed limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inherency is asserted, the burden shifts to the applicant to prove the prior art lacks the relied‑on characteristic. Cite case law (e.g., In re Schreiber, In re Swinehart). Examiners must make a prima facie showing and explain why the prior art structure inherently possesses the functional limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operation/recited intended use does not distinguish an apparatus claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim recitation regarding the manner in which an apparatus is intended to be employed (intended use) does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from a prior art apparatus if the prior art teaches all structural limitations of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended use or the way a device is employed is immaterial to structure; structural teachings in the prior art controlling. Example: Ex parte Masham — the Board affirmed rejection even though prior art used the device with different submersion because structure was the same. Examiner should focus on structural elements, not recited uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences control anticipation despite functional equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art device performs all functions recited in a claim, it does not anticipate the claim if there is any structural difference between the claimed apparatus and the prior art device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means‑plus‑function limitations are met by structures equivalent to those in the specification (e.g., In re Donaldson). Courts may construe claims to require discrete structural elements (e.g., In re Robertson — three fastening elements required despite reference performing same function with two). Examiners must compare structural limitations, and consider means‑plus‑function linkage to disclosed structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability analysis for computer‑implemented functional claim limitations (35 U.S.C. 102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; prior art that inherently performs the function may support a 102/103 rejection. Conversely, computer‑implemented functional limitations may narrow claims where hardware cannot meet limitations without enabling software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key considerations: (1) Functional claim language covering all capable devices — if prior art device can inherently perform the function, rejection may be appropriate (In re Translogic, Intel Corp. v. ITC, In re Schreiber, In re Best, In re Ludtke, In re Swinehart). (2) Claims may be construed to require a combination of hardware and enabling software where hardware alone cannot meet the limitation (Nazomi Communications v. Nokia). (3) The term 'computer' is commonly broad and should not be limited to specific characteristics absent definitional claim or specification language (In re Paulsen). (4) Broadly claiming automation of a manual function or implementing known functions on a general‑purpose computer can be obvious (Leapfrog, KSR, Muniauction); examiners should apply obviousness rationales (see MPEP §§2141, 2143 and exemplary rationales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material or article worked upon does not impart patentability to apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of the material or article worked upon by a claimed structure does not, without more, impart patentability to the claimed device; the device must be patentable based on its structural elements, not its intended article of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to machinery that work upon an article are limited to the machine's structure — the process or the article handled (e.g., hair being wound around a core) is irrelevant to machine patentability (In re Otto, In re Young, In re Casey). This line of cases is limited to claims directed to machinery that works upon an article in its intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel/nonobvious starting material or end product in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating obviousness of a process or method claim that recites making or using a novel/nonobvious product, the entire claim must be considered; there are no per se rules that a process is patentable merely because it yields a novel product or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 requires fact‑specific analysis considering all claim limitations (In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer, TorPharm v. Ranbaxy). A process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious; conversely, a process yielding a known product may be nonobvious. Treat product recitations as material limitations in claim construction. Review illustrative cases (In re Durden, Albertson, Kanter, Pleuddemann, Kuehl, Mancy) for precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim definition and general treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim recites a list of alternatively usable members (Markush grouping). Any claim that recites alternatively usable members, regardless of format, should be treated as a Markush claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markush style is common in chemistry, pharmacology, biology, and other fields but may also apply to mechanical features or process steps. A Markush grouping requires selection from a closed group (consisting of). See MPEP §2111.03 and §803.02 for election/search guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper Markush grouping requirements (single structural similarity and common use)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping is proper only if the members share both (1) a single structural similarity and (2) a common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two situations where a Markush grouping is ordinarily proper: (A) members belong to the same recognized physical/chemical class or art‑recognized class and are disclosed or known to be functionally equivalent and have a common use; (B) when alternatives are chemical compounds not in a recognized class, they may still be proper if they share a substantial structural feature essential to a common use. Examineors should determine substitutability — each member should be expected to achieve the same intended result. See case law (In re Harnisch, Ex parte Hozumi, In re Jones) and MPEP §2117 subsections II–IV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper Markush grouping — rejection and prosecution procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim is improper if members do not share a single structural similarity or a common use; such claims should be rejected on the merits under 'improper Markush grouping' principles (use Form Paragraph 8.40).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner actions/guidance: (1) Use form paragraph 8.40 and explain why alternatives fail to meet both requirements. (2) Make improper Markush grouping rejection in the first action on the merits after presentation of the claim (compact prosecution). (3) Require election of species for search/examination if appropriate (see MPEP §803.02). (4) Suggest ways to overcome rejection (present each alternative in separate claims, propose a proper grouping supported by the spec, or present convincing arguments of commonality). (5) Also consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) if skilled artisans cannot determine metes and bounds (indefiniteness). (6) Maintain rejection until claim is amended or convincing arguments presented; reconsider if record later shows members share structural similarity and common use. (7) No Markush claim can be allowed until improper grouping rejection is overcome or withdrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner guidance for drafting and explaining improper Markush rejections (Form Paragraph 8.40 content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form Paragraph 8.40 provides the template text and examiner notes for rejecting a claim on the basis of an improper Markush grouping and specifies the information to be filled in and reasons to provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the form paragraph to state which claim(s) are rejected, identify the improper grouping, and explain why the alternatives do not meet the requirements (e.g., not same recognized class, not functionally equivalent, or do not share substantial structural feature leading to common use). Include suggestions to applicant for overcoming rejection. If election of species is appropriate, only issue form paragraph after applicant election where required. Follow compact prosecution timing rules and include examiner notes for bracketed insertions (claim numbers, description of group, reasons).
